utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in the courtroom. This is case IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Today is Wednesday. Good afternoon, Ms. Bosanac. Good afternoon to the representatives of the OTP and to Mr. Seselj. We're going to proceed with the testimony of the witness. I still have a number of questions to put to you, Witness. I'm going to try to deal with the most relevant questions because we have another witness scheduled to testify after you. So I'm now going to focus only on the main issues, because I could go on and on putting all sorts of questions to you, but we are pressed for time and we need to focus on the most important matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We know you were the director at the hospital. At the hospital of Vukovar, did the director discharge medical and administrative duties, or was this only an administrative function?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time in 1991, in July 1991, I became the director of the Vukovar Medical Centre, which encompassed the hospital in Vukovar and all the other infirmaries, the health centres in charge of primary healthcare. At that time, I did administrative and organisational jobs. When it was necessary, I also examined children, being a pediatrician by specialisation. But it was predominantly administrative and organisational duties that were within my competence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You became the director of the hospital and the other health centres after having been appointed to that position or after having been elected?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The management body of the Vukovar Health Centre at that time was a body which was called the Workers Council, so I was elected by a vote on the part of the Workers Council and my appointment was endorsed by the Minister of Health.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Who was the person occupying your position before you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A doctor by the name Rade Popovic, chief physician, and he resigned to that post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why did Dr. Popovic resign that position or why was he forced to resign?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally cannot say with precision, but I do believe that at that time the situation was extremely difficult and complicated. The war had already started in our area, and I think that he simply did not want to perform that duty any longer, because it was a very difficult and exacting, demanding job; namely, that of organising the operation of a hospital amid a war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was Dr. Popovic a Serb, or a Croat, or was he a Muslim, a Yugoslav, or something else?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was Montenegrin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, he was Montenegrin. At the time when he resigned his position, were you aware of political tensions that pitted the Croats against the Serbs in the town of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was not pitted against them. He was one of those people who, amid all that tension which obtained after the 1991 spring elections in Vukovar, and he was on that occasion a candidate to be elected to the Croatian Assembly for the Chamber of Associated Labour, which was one of the chambers which existed at that time. Apart from that, he was one of the organisers of meetings of a group of intellectuals who regularly met. They were both Croats and Serbs and of different nationalities, their aim being to try and, together, see to the easing of the tensions. But needless to say, nobody heeded what they had to suggest, so that I don't think that he was in conflict with any particular group at that time but that he simply assessed that he would not be able to influence matters. He did say, however, that he would remain, that he would stay on, and he stayed on as the chief of the neuropsychiatry ward. But in August, he left to get his wife in Risan [phoen]. She also used to work in our hospital. And then he called us on the phone and he said that after all, he would not be able to return. And he was not at the Vukovar Hospital until the end of the war, he was in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, we've heard a great number of witnesses who told us about Vukovar. Among others, we heard a witness who was cross-examined by Mr. Seselj, who was asked by Mr. Seselj to confirm a number of events that took place in Vukovar, and I'm going to sum up because it's a rather long list of events. Serbs had been evicted by Croats. There were changes in the police personnel, Croats replaced Serbs, and the same happened in other institutions. There were cases of violence of Croats against the Serbs. In other words, there was a series of events that allegedly led to the departure of Kamenovic [phoen], head of the municipality, who was replaced. We've heard all this, and the witness was sitting where you're sitting today, confirmed that these events had indeed taken place. What about you? Were you aware of such events? Were you aware of such a behaviour of Croats against the Serbs that would have led to some people being evicted or expelled?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question is a general one. I can claim with full responsibility, because I was in Vukovar before the war, during the war, after the war, and on the 20th of November when Vukovar was occupied, so I claim that as far as I knew, there was no maltreatment whatsoever of Serbs, nor were they threatened or their jobs threatened in any way. I can state what I am certain about and what I experienced by myself, and that is the following: After Borovo Selo, when Croatian policemen were killed there, many Serbs failed to show up for work. Some of them left for Serbia. Others set up war health stations in the surrounding Serbian villages. When I was appointed director of the medical centre, I actually was not expecting this. But when I was nominated for that post, I accepted that challenge, and I thought that I would be able to organise the hospital to operate properly and to assist everybody. But the assistance which I had at the time -- allow me. I have to tell you this. The assistants of Director Popovic retained those posts; namely, Dr. Mladen Ivankovic, who was a Serb, and Mr. Njegovan Krstic, who was also a Serb. They were my assistants, and we continued working together on a daily basis; namely, many Serbs remained to work in the hospital until the end of the occupation, whereas many Croats also left the hospital and went to the free territories in Croatia, so that I cannot confirm that they were threatened in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I want to use the time we have as efficiently as possible, and I want to make sure that you answer my questions. Do you know a street in Vukovar that is called Dalmatinska Street?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know, more or less, where it is. It is near the barracks, the former barracks of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. During his cross-examination, the accused put the following question to the witness. I'm going to ask you the question myself. That's to be found at page 6713 of the transcript. The question was as follows: "Do you know that all Serb houses of Dalmatinska Street were searched and that the Serbs were all taken to the police station, where they were beaten up and some of them were killed?" Were you aware of these events? Did you hear about this?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I don't believe that that was so because this street is very near the barracks. That was already the frontline. So I had not heard of it and I don't believe it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me move on to the topic of the shelling of the hospital. We know that soldiers, injured soldiers, received treatment at the hospital. Was there a red cross drawn on the roof of the hospital so that it would be visible from the air, that everyone would know it was a hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were two red crosses. One red cross was on what is now the administrative building of the hospital, and another was in the courtyard, on the lawn. And the video cassettes which the OTP has visibly show it was a very conspicuous red cross and it was all pockmarked on account of the shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. In your written statement, you explained that the hospital was shelled for days on end by the JNA. Undoubtedly, your hospital was hit. But in your view, was this shelling targeting your hospital, in particular, or the town, in general?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is hard to say, because so many thousands of shells landed on the city on a daily basis, and I personally witnessed the demolition of everything left, right and center, so that I cannot say. But sometimes it seemed to us that we were -- precisely we were the target, targeted by rocket-launchers from the other bank of the Danube. Then there was aerial shelling of the entire city from Mitnica to Borovo Naselje, so that I don't think that exclusively the hospital was the target of the shelling. But it was certainly not excepted. The entire city was razed to the ground within the space of three months and practically totally demolished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We know, because you said it yourself, that you called the JNA and General Raseta, who was in Zagreb, and you called him to notify him of the shelling. Could you, very briefly, tell us exactly what General Raseta told you? Was he aware of the shelling? What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He behaved as if it was the first time he was hearing this and he didn't believe it. There was a relative of his with us in the hospital, a young man who wanted to talk to him, and he did talk to him, and he confirmed that we were being shelled. He asked for the shelling to abate, for helicopters to be sent for the wounded. However, that was all to no avail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here you are providing us with a very relevant piece of information. I was not aware of that myself. There was a cousin of General Raseta who talked to him on the phone and this relative of his confirmed that the hospital was, indeed, being shelled by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This cousin of his, was he a Serb, a Croat; what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I answer this question, could I ask for this session -- for us to go into closed session, because I have not talked with his family about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not a problem. Let's move into private session. One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll come back to that issue later. Witness, obviously General Raseta did nothing at all. Why is it that you didn't call the defence ministry in Belgrade to try and talk to someone there, someone who would be able to answer your call? Did you try to do it, were you unable to do it?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You did. Who did you speak to?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did ask, but I was unable to get through by direct line in Belgrade. Actually, it was through Zagreb that I got a number in Sarajevo, and I got the office of Admiral Brovet, who was in charge at that time. At least that is what I'd heard. I got this officer in the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army. I said who I was. I said that I was calling from Vukovar and that I was requesting them to stop shelling the hospital and the entire town. This officer told me that he couldn't let me speak to anyone else but that he would do some checking, that he didn't believe it, that the hospital was being shelled and so on. I told him to come in helicopter to Vukovar to see for himself, for themselves that the hospital was being shelled. They actually behaved as if they didn't believe it, and the truth was that they didn't want to hear it. I did my very best. I managed to establish many contacts with different people, but unfortunately I was unable to help stop the shelling, the devastation of Vukovar, the killing of the civilians there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I'm now going to deal with the evacuation of the hospital. Apparently, the evacuation was negotiated at meetings between the JNA, the Croatian Army and various international organisations. It was thus decided to evacuate the hospital. Did you yourself have fears about what would happen during the evacuation or after the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally have to say while these negotiations were being conducted, when in the early morning on the 17th I heard that the evacuation would start on the 18th, I was confident that it would indeed be carried out exactly according to the agreement, that the International Red Cross and European Monitors would come to the hospital and that we would evacuate all the wounded, the sick and all the civilians from the hospital on that day. It was a Monday, the 18th, and the evacuation of Borovo Naselje was to be carried out on the 19th. There was a standby hospital there in Borovo Naselje with also quite a few patients and civilians there. And on the 20th, the Wednesday, all the other civilians who were not wounded and sick were to be evacuated. That was the information I had, and that was my hope. On Monday morning, when no one showed up at the hospital, nor called us or reported in any way, I started worrying and I started making calls and asking for the Minister of Health to see what was happening. At 11.00 on that day, the European Monitors Mission people called me and they told me that they could not come to the hospital as agreed because they were not allowed to do so. That same day, Minister Hebrang told me that he informed by the International Red Cross that they were en route and that they were near the hospital but that they were busy surrendering or handing over Croatian soldiers in the southern part of the city. I didn't know what he was talking about, but later I understood that neither the Red Cross or the -- nor the European Mission was able to comply with the signed agreement, because to get to the city in the first place, they would have had to obtain permission from the person then in charge, who was Major Sljivancanin, and he wouldn't let them go inside the city. He first took them to Mitnica, where the Croatian soldiers from Mitnica were surrendering, and only after that, on Tuesday, when the army had already entered and with it the paramilitary units and the different ilk of volunteers, it was only at dusk on the 19th that the representative of the International Red Cross managed to arrive at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The representative of the International Red Cross came to the hospital on the 19th. Can you tell us, very briefly, what he did, and why he did not stay at the hospital, and why he left?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came, brought a lorry full of medical supplies and medicines and they were brought by Major Sljivancanin. They inspected the hospital. They looked at all the lists of the wounded that we had prepared. I had a very unpleasant surprise when this gentleman, Nikola, said that they were going back to Belgrade but would come back in the morning. Why they hadn't stayed, you would have to ask him, because already that same night many people were taken away from the hospital, never to be seen again, and they were not found even at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in your view, if the International Community had been there through its representatives, through the European Mission, the Red Cross, MSF, what have you, would that have changed the course of events or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it would. However, the European Monitors would have had to come to the hospital and stayed there, and the ICRC would have had to come to the hospital and stayed there, because the agreement clearly states they would handle the evacuation of the hospital. But as I said, the person in charge in the field of all that at the time was Major Sljivancanin, and he simply didn't make sure it happened. Mr. Borsinger, when he came, he saw buses on the other side of the street. These buses were taking people to Ovcara. He saw them, and he wanted to list the people. But Major Sljivancanin countered aggressively. He said it was his country, not Borsinger's country, so the people were not listed. And all I can say is if the European Monitors and the ICRC people had been there, the crime would not have happened, which of course does not detract from the responsibility and guilt of those who killed civilians, over 1.500 civilians of all nationalities before the evacuation and then after the evacuation, many more wounded, sick people, civilians who were killed before eyewitnesses, and there are testimonies to that. I have to tell you that the people in Vukovar were very disappointed by the judgement of this Tribunal in the case of Veselin Sljivancanin and Mr. Radic, because we hold Mr. Sljivancanin to have been the person who decided on the life and death of all those in the Vukovar Hospital who were eventually massacred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The indictment against this accused, we have the subject of Vukovar as well, so that this Trial Chamber will have to assess what happened in reality. There is no doubt about it, individuals were killed in Ovcara. Nobody challenges that; neither does the accused. It's just that the Judges will have to make a decision, will have to decide who did that and why they did that. This is going to be our problem, and we'll have to settle this after due deliberation. This is why we have witnesses who come to testify, and you are one of them. The accused has a theory; other witnesses, too. It is the theory that the events that took place in Vukovar allegedly were carried out by members of the local TO who, as it were, took revenge on the prisoners and allegedly have committed those crimes. What do you think of the case put by the accused?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What can I tell you? I gave it a lot of thought, why in precisely that way, why precisely those people, and I'm not the only one who has been thinking about that. There are whole institutes in Croatia grappling with the matter. The fact is I can speak only of Vukovar. About Kostajnica, about Skabrnja and other locations, I cannot speak because all I know is from reading. Vukovar is what I know about. I know that both the army, the paramilitaries, the reservists and the volunteers and what do you call them, the Territorial Defence, now already ex-citizens of Vukovar, they all acted in unison. They could have done nothing on their own if the army hadn't shelled and bombed the town. Without the army, they could not have done anything. The army destroyed the town, and just as they protected some of the wounded, 164 of them from the hospital, and protected the wounded from Borovo Komerc company, like they protected and arrested some of us from the Vukovar Hospital like myself and Mr. Njavro, they could have protected and saved everyone. The Army, then represented by Veselin Sljivancanin, and all the other units under the control of this accused who is sitting here and listening, if they had wanted to protect the wounded, they could have. They simply sacrificed them in order to take their revenge, I don't really know why, for the failure they had experienced, because they had been saying that Vukovar would fall within a month. I personally heard Sljivancanin say on the radio that, "Vukovar will fall within a month. We will plough over everything, make a park in its place." And then when it didn't happen and when the massacre happened instead, he simply let the soldiers take it all out on our compatriots, on the wounded, on the sick.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you have just expressed your point of view, and it has been recorded in the transcript. Several witnesses have testified. Others will come as well. Some of them seem, I do say "seem," to show that at some point in time the regular forces of the JNA, including the military police and some JNA officers, that they were totally overwhelmed by the events and by the acts of some individuals, including some members of the TO, or some volunteers who were on location. What do you think? Do you think this is a credible point of view or not at all; that is, that it might be that the JNA was just overwhelmed and overtaken by other people?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean "overwhelmed"? If they had wanted to, they had the weapons, they had the power, they could have carried out the evacuation as it should have been done if they had wanted to, I say, but they didn't want to, as -- just as they sent some of the wounded in an evacuation convoy to Croatia, that same way they could have taken those buses and those civilians and sent them not to Ovcara but to Croatia. You can't say they didn't know it or they wanted to but couldn't. They sent them to Ovcara for a purpose. They knew what was going on there. It was widely known, not only in Vukovar. The same or similar happened in many other places, and there are still survivors and witnesses who managed to get out of there with their head on their shoulders and who pointed out the locations of mass graves, although not all the dead have been found. 494 people are still missing from Vukovar, and 262 of them are missing of those who were in the hospital. So if you ask me, the army that had entered the town was able to control all of its troops, but it simply let things go and allowed for the massacre to happen. I personally saw the autopsy report for my father-in-law, which notes an entry and exit wound to the head, which means it was an execution. It couldn't have happened without the knowledge and consent of those who came into and occupied the city. That means all the troops of the army and the reservists who acted shoulder to shoulder with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There seems to be a mistake in the transcript on line 3 -- on lines 3 and 4, page 16. There is a mention of a certain amount of people, 494, and then 262. And if I understood you properly, you said that there was 62 people who still are missing to date.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said 262 persons are missing from the hospital. 200 were found in Ovcara and 62 were still missing. And if you take Vukovar and the surrounding area, 494 people are missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So to date, 494 people from Vukovar and the surrounding area have not been found. Out of this figure, there are 62 people who had been in the hospital. Thank you for making this clear. One last topic, your own detention in the Sremska Mitrovica prison. We have your statement and we learn that you were detained until the 8th of December, 1992. Could you explain why you were detained? First of all, tell us who arrested you and detained you, on what grounds, and how you were released.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, the 20th, in the morning - it was a Wednesday, 7.00 - I was again at the Vukovar Hospital after spending the night in Negoslavci, being interrogated before Sljivancanin at their headquarters in Negoslavci, and then in the morning Vidic and I were taken back to the hospital, and at 7.00 Sljivancanin said we had to convene a meeting in a large room of all the medical staff. So at 7.30, we all met in the plaster room, where he addressed us and said that the hospital would be taken over by the Military Medical Academy. There were seven or eight doctors there in military uniforms who took over the running of the hospital, and all the others were told they could either go to Croatia or stay in Vukovar, as they wished. One soldier or, rather, officer of the JNA - I don't know rank - took Marin Vidic and myself to the barracks, saying that we were going to agree with the ICRC about an evacuation. It was around 7.00, 8.00 in the morning when we were taken to the barracks, and we were kept there under the guard of the military police until that evening. I was interrogated, and then I was put, without any explanation, into a prison vehicle, where I found Mr. Njavro and another technician, and we drove towards Belgrade, as far as we could see through a small window. And then we were taken around 2.00 a.m. to Sremska Mitrovica, to the prison, where I went through the torture of prisoners. One colonel of the JNA met us there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Witness. We'll get to that later. Let me return to something you said. So you were put in front of cameras. I suppose you were recorded, filmed. Was it the army recording or was it the Belgrade TV or CNN? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the army. I didn't see any civilians there. Everybody was in uniform. It was like a filmed statement, where I said who I was, what I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you were taken to the prison, and you said you were tortured there. We'll speak about this in a moment. When you were detained, were you told of an indictment, were you told what the charges were against you, was there a military investigative judge who came to see you, or were you just sort of put in a cell without any reason?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was put in an isolation cell in that prison in Sremska Mitrovica, a very cold, dirty isolation cell where I spent that night, and the next day I was placed in a room with some women who were also from Vukovar, women from Mitnica and Sajmiste, 66 women in one room. So I was there with them, and every day I was interrogated by one colonel named Branko, whose -- in fact, I asked him what I was charged with, why I was in prison, and he said I was there to make a statement about what was going on in Vukovar. So there I wrote a statement which is also available here at the Tribunal. I believe it was on 22 pages -- 92 pages. I kept asking him when I would be released, whether I would be allowed to go back to Vukovar, because I wanted to know what happened to my husband. The ICRC delegation came a few days later. European Monitors found me in that prison three or four days later. I was there in Sremska Mitrovica until the 10th, writing that statement, and that colonel kept saying that as soon as I'm done with the statement, I would be going to Zagreb. While I was still writing the statement - it was a Sunday - they came suddenly and told me to pack, that I'm leaving, and then I spent another two days in the investigating prison in Belgrade, and there I appeared before some sort of trial chamber. There was one prosecutor, one judge, and they asked me if I wanted defence counsel, to which I said, "What am I charged with, in the first place?" They said the charge would probably be armed insurgency, and I replied I'd never held a weapon, nor had I ever done any harm to anyone, and, "What does it mean," I said. "Am I supposed to take defence counsel from here at the prison?" They said one would be appointed, and then a person appeared in uniform who was allegedly a defence counsel. And then they went through those appeals that I had written, where I clearly wrote that the Yugoslav People's Army was destroying Vukovar, and that's what they were holding against me, basically. However, they didn't bring any charges. Instead, I stayed in that isolation cell until Tuesday, and the others who were brought from Mitrovica and Nis, including some doctors and priests, and my husband was in that group as well, they were also in that military investigation prison in Belgrade. And then, nevertheless, on Tuesday they put us on a bus, then on a plane, and we were exchanged as prisoners of war for some people who had been arrested in Zagreb. I don't know what they were called, some sort of Laborador group, some spies. In any case, we were exchanged for them, and that's how 13 days later I came to Zagreb and later learned that at that time the US ambassador, whose name eludes me at the moment - maybe it's Zimmerman -- anyway, Professor Hebrang and President Tudjman asked that physicians, priests be released from prisons, so we were eventually exchanged 13 days later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the beginning, you said that you had been tortured. Was there a mistake, did I mishear? When you were detained, was there any act of physical violence against you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depends on what you understand "physical violence" to mean. I was not abused in terms of beating, except when we were escorted as a group and then the guards would hit us, not minding where and whom they hit, but the whole detention was torture to me, abuse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us speak about Colonel Branko, this famous Colonel Branko. He asked you to produce a statement. Did he then say that it had to be geared towards saying something specific or were you absolutely free to say everything that had happened in the most free possible way?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, he specifically told me to write, in chronological order, what had happened, with whom I made contact, what I know about various people, what I knew about fighting men, their names, and I wanted to write the truth as I perceived it then, and that's how I started. However, he warned me that that would not be good, the way I was writing it, and the fact is I started writing the statement in the same way I wrote my appeals, describing all that we had gone through during the war. But he told me that that was no good, I had to state who I had cooperated with, whom I had called in Zagreb. It was a kind of questioning, except I had to write my answers down; whom I had contacted abroad, outside Croatia, all the people whom I had called on the telephone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you had this interview with Colonel Branko. Did he want to know what kind of contacts you'd had with Colonel Raseta or with the JNA? Was he interested in that or not at all?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he wasn't particularly interested. What he wanted to know was the people whom I had contact with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did he then speak with you about the fate of the people who had been evacuated from the hospital, including the fate of those who found themselves at Ovcara, or did he say nothing about it? He didn't say anything, did he?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is going to be my last question, and I'll see whether my colleagues have questions themselves. You answered, "No." I can see that in the transcript on line 19, page 21, the answer was not recorded. You answered with a, "No." So that's corrected. So, Witness, this is going to be my last question, after which I'll give the floor to my colleagues, if they have questions themselves. So following all these events, did you write one or many books? We know that there is one book called the appeals, the appeals that you had made, but did you write other books, other than that one? And if so, what were the titles?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Last year, we published a monograph entitled "The Vukovar Hospital, 1991." It's on 360 pages, and it also covers a history of the Vukovar area and the history of the Vukovar Hospital, everything that happened in 1991 in the Vukovar Hospital. And at the end of the book, there are photographs of all the people who were killed in Ovcara, people from the Vukovar Hospital who are still on record as missing, then reminiscences of wounded children, wounded soldiers. And I turned over that book to the Prosecution as well, that book that was published in Croatia last year, but I have also prepared here a copy for you, personally. This year, we prepared an English edition, and on the 18th of November, which is the day of remembrance for Vukovar in Croatia, this book will appear in English. There are just a few contributions of mine in that book. It's not my book. It was co-authored by many people who worked in and for the Vukovar Hospital. So when you have time to read it, maybe some things will become much clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, you are now working again in the Vukovar Hospital. This hospital is now running today with doctors, with medical staff, administrative staff, with nurses and other staff. Are there Croats, Serbs, or people of other nationalities in the staff or you only have Croats on the staff?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you well know, in 1998, by virtue of the agreement on peaceful reintegration of the Danube area in Croatia, Vukovar was again integrated into Croatia. I was the director of the Vukovar Hospital in exile, and I participated in the process of peaceful reintegration. And in the summer of 1998, I first came back to the Vukovar Hospital. In 1996, I had been in Vukovar already for the first negotiations, but in 1998 I returned to the hospital. I found the city almost completely destroyed. The hospital was partly rebuilt. And we fully implemented that agreement on peaceful reintegration, which included keeping on all the personnel who was working in that medical centre now called Sveti Save in 1996. That included the hospital and the primary healthcare centre. We cooperated with the UN, after that with the European Monitors, in the implementation of that agreement. However, leaving them alone, the most important thing to me in 1991 and today is that all the personnel, regardless of ethnicity and faith, should do their jobs as best as possible, to the best their ability, and treat all the patients in the best possible way, regardless, again, of ethnicity, faith, or any other affiliation. Nowadays, the hospital employs 520 staff members of various ethnicities. Some were -- some are from Serbia, some are from Croatia, some worked during the occupation in Vukovar and stayed on, while others returned. Regardless of everything we had been through, none of my colleagues or myself believed that ethnicity matters. What matters is how good the doctor is, how able he is to help the patients. I believe we have succeeded in our efforts, and the hospital is now entering the last stage of rebuilding and renovation, which will be over in two years. And Vukovar by that time, I hope, will also be completely rebuilt. There are people of all ethnicities and faiths living in Vukovar today. It used to have a population of 45.000. Nowadays the population is 32.000. I believe Vukovar has a future. However, we will never forget the past. We've just learned to live with it. There are several memorials and museums in Vukovar keeping the memory of the suffering of people during the war and the occupation of Vukovar. And in our own hospital, we have an area which is a small museum to commemorate the victims of 1991. 18.000 people have visited this little museum in the hospital. School children, retirees, teachers, lawyers, are among the visitors, bishops as well. There was a recent ecumenical conference of Catholic priests in Belgrade, and from Belgrade they came to our hospital to see this museum. And I brought invitations to you as well, and I want to hand them to you, and I believe that you will understand much better all that happened and what it looks like today, once you've visited Vukovar and our hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm now going to turn to my fellow Judges to see if they have questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, I have just a few questions to you which relate to the role of the paramilitaries during the occupation of the hospital. Now, you say in your statement that you saw the paramilitaries, the soldiers and Chetniks, for the first time on the 19th of November, and I understand that on that day and in the following days, a number of the paramilitaries took part in the action that occurred at the hospital. Is that correct? Just to check that I have understood correctly.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm interested to know or to learn from you what you could observe regarding the coordination between the soldiers and the paramilitaries, the Chetniks, the volunteers. Were you able to form an impression about who controlled them, or did you see anyone giving orders to them, or did they perhaps just act on their own and did they seem to you to be independent of the soldiers? Did you have any impression of how their actions were coordinated with the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I can be precise in answering this question. What I saw and what I could feel, for instance, when the troops of the army entered the hospital, there was an officer of the army who came to the hospital. I went out and I asked them whether they were being accompanied by the ECMM and the Red Cross, and he said, "No." And I told him we were expecting the International Red Cross, according to the agreement, and he told me that he knew nothing about it. Then I asked him, "Who is the one who does know," because I would have to get in touch with someone who knew where the International Red Cross was. Then he told me that he had seen some EU monitors and some ICRC representatives in Negoslavci. Then, of my own accord, I went to Negoslavci. I asked them to take me there so I could get in touch with the Red Cross. But before that, I asked him whether he could vouch, say that no one would enter the hospital of the troops or anybody else until the Red Cross people came, and he told me, yes, he could guarantee that, and he designated some people to stand guard at the entrance to the hospital. They were to wait there until the International Red Cross people arrived. But I also know that when I was taken back from Negoslavci, that I saw reservists barging into the hospital, paramilitary unit members with helmets on their heads entering the hospital, barging into the hospital, and on their helmets were some markings, some Chetnik insignia with some white ribbons. That was no regular army. There was no regular army there. There were some regular troops outside, but they did not prevent them from entering. So I went outside, and I tried to prevent them from entering the hospital, but they obviously had not recognised me and they actually paid no heed to me, but they did recognise a surgeon of ours whose son was in these units, and he came out and he told them not to go inside the hospital. When they were taking me to Negoslavci, with us rode a Chetnik, as I say, in the car. This was an unkempt man with a fur hat, a bearded man, in boots and with a huge knife tucked into his belt, and he looked at me and this man volatile, with so much hatred that I was -- I was sure if we had not been in this military vehicle that he would have killed us. The moment he realised that we were from the hospital, he had such a feeling of hatred that I could see that he told the driver, "Stop, I want to get out." He just couldn't bear to ride in the car with us. So it is hard to say now what people could have told other people and who was commanding other people or could have ordered somebody else. It is hard to say now. It's simply, in my view, the army had taken the city, and let them do whatever they pleased. I told this Colonel Branko that I don't have to show him exactly where we took our dead and deposited them until we could bury them, and he told me openly that it would not be wise for me to do so because we would not be able to leave Vukovar alive. If that is truth, for that matter, so I can't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's just be sure about who is who. The impression you leave with me is that the soldiers of the JNA were easily recognisable by their uniform, whereas the paramilitaries and the volunteers were equally easily recognisable by their being dressed more leniently, only partly uniformed, and perhaps with insignia, or fur hats, or by other recognisable traces. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sorry. So you were able to distinguish clearly who was a JNA soldier and who was a volunteer or a paramilitary?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I think that I was able to distinguish between them, but I cannot claim that it was like that in every situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. But the general picture was that the volunteers could, generally speaking, easily be recognised and distinguished from the JNA soldiers. Let me then ask you if you --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My impression is the army came in and passed. I cannot say, because I was taken to prison, but according to the testimonies of many people and of many women whose stories I heard in prison, the army came and went. These people went into these cellars, shouting, "Get out. If you do not get out, we are going to throw a bomb," so that people got out of the basements. They pushed them, loaded them onto vehicles, drove them away. Some people survived, others didn't. Many are missing. The fates of many others are unknown. They singled out people from the column in plain sight of the soldiers, in plain sight of the people who were responsible, who were supposed to be responsible for the evacuation. They took people away, and nothing is known of them to this day. This is -- these are the stories that I heard from eyewitnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I see. And when you say "these people went into these cellars," and so on, by "these people," you mean the paramilitaries or the volunteers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's who I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Now, I wanted also to ask you about the approximate distribution of soldiers and volunteers. Can you give me any impression of how many the volunteers were in comparison to the soldiers? Was it about half, half of the military persons who entered the hospital were soldiers, and the other half were volunteers or --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I saw, among those who arrived at the hospital and those whom I met as I was taken to Negoslavci, from Negoslavci, and to prison, there were many, many more regular troops there, armoured personnel carriers, tanks. I just couldn't believe the number of tanks. Even though we were being destroyed and razed to the ground, I just couldn't believe their numbers, the numbers of the APCs. I believe there must have been -- what I saw, I mean, the ratio between the regular troops and the paramilitaries must have been 20 to 1 in favour of the regular army, except that it is my impression that the army just went in and was anxious to leave as soon as possible, and they just went out. But I am quite sure that had they wanted to preserve those wretched, poor civilians, sick civilians, among whom there were also Serbs because there were hundreds of people in the cellars of Vukovar, a third of whom were Serbs, had they genuinely wanted then preserved, the army would have evacuated them properly. But, no, these other people did as they pleased. And when they emerged from the cellars and when they saw that there were also Serbs among the people who came out of the cellars, they would separate them. Some of them would shout as they were coming out, "I'm a Serb," and in respect of others, actually, others got beaten because they were shouting, "I'm a Serb," because they asked them, "What are you doing with a Ustasha, then, if you are a Serb?" In the magazine "Vreme" which I brought, in an interview of 6 November, the accused wrote that not a single Ustasha can leave Vukovar alive, and in his book, every Serb even who was with Ustasha was also Ustasha.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We'll get to that in a minute. Can I just ask you about the ratio between JNA soldiers and the volunteers? You told us it was about 20 to 1, and my question is precise: Was that same ratio applicable to --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my impression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand, but my question is: Was that same ratio also applicable to the group of armed persons at the hospital? Do you understand my question? Because I thought you said that when you went outside the hospital, you were able to see that there were many more JNA soldiers than there were volunteers, and my question then refers you back to the hospital, during those days when you were there. And my question is: At the hospital, were there also an equal -- the same ratio of soldiers and volunteers; that is to say, about 20 to 1?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: My last question is related to the leadership that you have testified about. We have heard you say at several occasions, and this is also in your statements, that General Mrksic was -- Colonel Mrksic was there, and also Sljivancanin, yet I think you also testified yesterday when you were asked by the Presiding Judge who controlled the volunteers, and your answer to that, if I'm not mistaken, was that that was the accused. So this raises the issue of: What did you actually mean? If Mrksic and Sljivancanin were in control of the operation, then how could the accused also be in control of the operation? So my question to you is: What did you actually mean, and on which basis did you tell us yesterday that the accused was in control?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I talked with General Raseta, he told me that within the framework of the evacuation of the hospital -- actually, Colonel Milorad Mrksic was responsible for that. When I called him on the 19th on Tuesday to ask how come nobody had shown up, not the Red Cross or anybody else, then he told me Colonel Milan Mrksic will find you, and indeed he did call me on the phone. He told me that he knew me, that we knew each other, that he also was from Vukovar, and that I shouldn't worry. And I said, "How shall I not worry? People are dying of gangrene. We have no food, we have no water, there have been -- nobody has come to see us in two days." So the information I got was that the commander of that entire sector was Milan Mrksic. And when they took me to Negoslavci, which is what I asked for in order to see the Red Cross people and their staff, Milan Mrksic was there at a desk, and he said that the International Red Cross would come there immediately, that he would send water tanks. And then they took me back to the hospital again, and that was the first time I saw Sljivancanin with a group of soldiers driving out civilians from the first floor, civilians who had not been in the hospital before that day. I asked them what they were doing, that we had to evacuate the hospital first, and he just shrugged off arrogantly, shooed me away, said it was none of my business. And so they took all these civilians and put them onto lorries. That was on the afternoon of the 19th, the Tuesday. So I understood that Sljivancanin was the man in charge in the field, and that other guy over there [indicates]. Why did I say this? Because I -- the accused. I heard with my very own ears, when he came to Vukovar before in October and November, I heard him encouraging Serbian soldiers, whether they were volunteers or any other unit members, that he encouraged them, and that is why I saw him as the leader. Sljivancanin was the uniformed leader. That is why I said so, and that is what I still maintain today. The ideatic [as interpreted] leader was the accused. I said so to this person who was guarding me in the Staff. I don't know what his name was. I'm talking about my own Crisis Staff. I said that they were doing everything that Seselj said, and he said to me, "Why are you saying that? The troops are not doing what Seselj does." And I told him, "Oh, yes, they are, they certainly are," because I heard him say that Vukovar would be razed to the ground and a park installed in its place, and that's exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sorry, I did not get that. Did you hear the accused say that Vukovar would be razed to the ground?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Where did you hear this?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On radio, on radio, whilst I was still in Vukovar, over the radio. We listened to the Serbian radio, we tuned in to the Serbian radio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dutertre, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two matters of procedure I would like to raise, and I have two questions as part of the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Redirect can only take place after cross-examination. As there has been no cross-examination, there cannot be any redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but since the Judges put questions to the witness, the Prosecutor may like to explore some of the issues raised by the Judges. Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have two follow-up questions following the questions you put, yourself, to the witness about the level of organisation of all this and the fact that the JNA may have been overtaken by events.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness, you were the director of the hospital during the conflicts. Some people died at the hospital, and you were called on to take the necessary steps to have these people buried. I suppose you're familiar with the steps that need to be taken to arrange a burial. Could you please tell me, based on your experience, what sort of organisation you need to bury 200 bodies?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you need -- actually, when we saw that it was impossible to bury the dead in the cemeteries, we had an excavator dig a grave next to the old cemetery, and we started burying the people there. But it was a problem, because under the shower of shells, the excavator was unable to work. I'm not quite sure, actually, what you mean by "organisation," but it was not easy to organise. We made lists, we had coffins made. The Borovo factory made the coffins for the dead. Everything was very difficult to do under the shells. When we no longer managed to do even that, we would just deposit them by the hospital and mark them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I'm going to rephrase my question to make it clearer. We know that 200 persons died at Ovcara. What degree of organisation do you need to bury 200 bodies in the mass grave at Ovcara? How much organisation do you need?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wouldn't necessarily have to have been a very high degree of organisation. First of all, we would have to load all those onto buses, as they were loaded onto buses, six buses, and then take them to Ovcara, and then there was this excavator that came and dug this hole, and then they took them by lorries and had them -- over to that spot and had them executed. This was not done by Territorials only. Of that I'm certain. It had to be a deliberate, well-thought-out action on the part of all of them, including the army. In fact, Sljivancanin told me, when he was interrogating me -- he asked me where the Croatian soldiers were, the Jastreb, the hawks, and I asked him why did you bring them here in the first place, "Why did you bring your men here in the first place, to demolish Vukovar and to get killed in Vukovar."

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions, Your Honour, but let me raise two points very quickly. First of all, the 92 ter statement of the witness was tendered and bears number P587. I would like to ask the Chamber to put this document or exhibit under seal. We have the same statement here, the same 92 ter statement that has been redacted, and it bears identification number ID 0641-9417-RED, for "redaction." I seek to tender this document as the public exhibit, and I seek a number for that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This was to answer concerns about confidentiality and relatives and medical matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Registrar, you need to state that Exhibit P587 is under seal and we need a new number for exhibit ID 0641-9417-RED. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, redacted version of exhibit P587 becomes Exhibit P603, and P587 is placed under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, P603.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 26, line 18, Dr. Bosanac said something that was not recorded on the transcript. I'd like us to move briefly into closed session to deal with this, because this raises an issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Dutertre, but this is on the recording, on the audio recording, and the transcript then will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but, you know, I knew who was mentioned, but I believe that the name was not properly recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, on behalf of my fellow Judges, I would like to thank you for having testified over these past two days about the events that took place in Vukovar. Let me thank you on behalf of the Trial Chamber. I wish you a safe trip home back to Vukovar and to the hospital, where you work as a director. We're going to have a break, and after this 20-minute break we'll hear the next witness. Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the part regarding line 18 -- lines 18 and following will be redacted from page 36. This witness testified under oath. You were free to cross-examine her, and you decided not to because of a principle of yours. All we can do now is say that her testimony is over. Our apologies for this incident, Witness. What has been said is going to be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, can the redaction --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... no legal grounds to redact my words from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the Trial Chamber decides that it should be redacted. It is now 10 to 4.00. We're going to have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, before the next witness comes into the courtroom, the Prosecution wants it put on the record, in the most clearest possible terms, that the outburst by the accused is unacceptable, and we would strongly recommend the Trial Chamber to caution him against such future outbursts. This is not the first time the accused has made statements concerning witnesses that are derogatory. This is exactly why the Prosecution has sought to impose counsel upon the accused, and we would argue and submit that the behaviour of the accused shortly before the break is but the most recent in a string of such outrageous and improper behaviour that clearly merits the imposition of Defence counsel as quickly as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj, what has just been said by Mr. Mundis is against you. He has just said that statements against witnesses justify the imposition of counsel upon you, and he strongly recommends the Trial Chamber to caution you against such outbursts. Witnesses come to testify. We have two categories of witnesses, the viva voce ones, and you cross-examine them, and we have 92 ter witnesses. You've decided not to cross-examine the latter. You have noticed that the Trial Chamber is very vigilant when it comes to 92 ter witnesses. We do ask questions that you, yourself, could have asked. But if we do ask a question, it is because we want truth to be expressed, to be manifested, as much as possible. We do our job the best we can. It may be that we do not ask questions that you could have asked, because you have other information. That is possible. We do not know everything you do know. But based on everything we have available, based on witnesses' answers, we do try to go to the heart of the matter. It may be that you do not like all the answers provided by witnesses. We can understand that, but that is not a good enough reason for you to attack a witness or to express reproaches, even if you think that a witness did not tell the truth or tried to avoid an issue. That may be the case, but this is a judicial debate, a discussion, a proceeding in which all parties have to behave properly. The Prosecutor is going to put questions. You will have questions. Sometimes you do not like the Prosecution's questions, you object to them. On several occasions the Trial Chamber asked the Prosecution to reformulate their question, and vice versa. It may happen that you ask questions and that that raises objections by the Prosecution. Sometimes we told you to proceed because you were right in asking that question. At other times, we asked you to reformulate them. So we do our best to make sure that the proceedings unfold as smoothly as possible. Admittedly, for the time being we are having Prosecution witnesses at the stand, and they are not called in order to say that you are innocent. If they are called, it's because in the Prosecution's view, they are witnesses that are going to speak against you. You may not like it. That's understandable enough, but the fact that you have a Prosecution witness at the stand does not mean that you can attack the witness. You should not behave in this way. In the Prosecutor's view, if you had a counsel, we could avoid this kind of problem. It is true that it could avoid this kind of problem, but the reverse could be true as well. The fact that you have a lawyer does not mean that you're not going to be on your feet and attack a witness. That's the problem, that's where the problem lies. Once again, Mr. Seselj, do try and get a grip on yourself. Only use your words efficiently. You can say that you do not agree with what a witness says, but limit it to that, and that's much more effective than if you get out of bounds and say, as you said before, the things that you said before the break, because each and every time you're going to have the Prosecutor on his feet to say what he's just said, and I have to give you the floor for you to answer, for several weeks already. And I'm under the very clear impression that things were going better and better all the time. The hearings were taking place very well, I should say that to you and recognise that, but what happened before the break should not have occurred. It is true that for several weeks already, I thought that there was a change, things were going better, normally as they should take place or could take place in your country and mine. There was no problem at all, and all of a sudden we had this problem before the break. So, Mr. Seselj, I do invite you once again to do what you have done so far; ask your questions whenever they're necessary, if you're not happy with something, just say so, but do not attack witnesses. You may have witnesses of good faith. Some of them might be against you, but this is not a reason why you should attack them, because when you call your own witnesses, the Prosecution is not going to attack them. If they do so, well, they will be told by the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber will tell them that they are not entitled to accuse the Defence witnesses of being this or that. But the Prosecutor will cross-examine your witnesses. If the Prosecutor were to say the same things as what you said about the last witness, the Trial Chamber would intervene. This is what I wanted to convey to you. Maybe we can remain at that, unless you want to say something, and you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, I'm convinced that in this courtroom, at least in this courtroom, I am the quietest and the most composed man, and all that I have said concerning the testimony of Vesna Bosanac under 92 ter, at the end of her testimony, I said quietly, and I was very composed when I said it. Without any legal grounds, you erased it from the transcript, but that's up to you. I can't change anything about it. But I warn you, in the system of adversarial proceedings, much harsher things are allowed to be said to witnesses. What I said was so innocuous, compared to what can be said. Let me remind you of Oscar Wilde's trial. That's a textbook example of how cross-interrogation can be done. I did not cross-interrogate at all -- cross-examine at all. I just made one remark when the examination of Vesna Bosanac was complete. What I said about Vesna Bosanac is the opinion of the entire Serbian public, knowing well her actions in the Vukovar Hospital during the war. Now, let me tell you, I sat in this box, this same box, as a witness in the Milosevic trial. Jeffrey Nice was allowed to say all kinds of things to me at the time. At one point, he said that I am a very vicious and evil man. Find it in the transcript. Let me not repeat the other things. Of course, I talked back to him, but this is just an example of what the Prosecutor was allowed to tell me. I have transcripts from other trials and examples of what the Prosecutor said to other witnesses who were taken aback and did not know how to defend themselves. This is just a procedure that facilitates the parading of witnesses through this courtroom. I did not cause an incident. I just said, calmly and composedly, what I wanted to be entered into the record concerning her testimony. Prosecutor Dutertre caused an incident. He jumped up, started waving his arms, flailing and shouting uncontrollably. And now the crux of this matter, Judges. You said that you asked the questions that I did not want to ask, that I would have asked if I had exercised my right to cross-examine. That is not true. You do not know in advance what questions I would have asked. However, you have in front of you the written statement compiled by the Prosecution and signed by Vesna Bosanac. Based on that written statement, in spite of all my warnings and demands on several occasions, you accepted her testimony to go in under 92 ter. The fact that you accepted her under 92 ter obliged you to make sure that her testimony stay within the scope of the written statement, whereas you extended her evidence by asking her about things that the Prosecutor omitted to write in the statement. All the questions that you asked, you and your colleague Judge Harhoff, and especially her answers, if they had been in her written statement before, I think would have put you off admitting her under 92 ter. You would have made her a viva voce witness. There is an essential problem here, not of my doing. I caused only a procedural problem because I believe that you unlawfully allowed witnesses to be introduced under 92 ter. I explained my reasons several times, and that is wrong. But the essential problem is the witness is appearing under 92 ter, the Prosecution is given half an hour, considerably exceeded by the Prosecutor, it was actually an hour, an hour and a half, maybe two hours - the Registry knows - and then with the questions from the Trial Chamber, it was prolonged to a whole day and one session. My reckoning is that it was five hours, at least, instead of the half an hour earlier planned. And then this begs the question: Why was it under 92 ter at all if it took five hours? Why couldn't my two hours fit in that, or an hour, which would have been possible if she had testified in the courtroom about the matters asked by the Prosecutor. You see what she says? She listened on Radio Sabac, to me saying that not a single Ustasha should be allowed out alive because she allegedly read about it in the newspaper. Somebody fabricated that subsequently, because that's the part where the Prosecution is missing evidence. One witness said I held a speech in front of the Command of Radic's company, another says about my speech in Leva Supoderica, another says he had me walking through Vukovar, and yet another says that he overheard in Vukovar that not a single Ustasha must be allowed out alive. You have four different testimonies, and all that is coming in while I am not able to react adequately. I warned the Prosecution sufficiently while I was still submitting evidence for translation, I have a huge number of newspaper articles speaking specifically of Vesna Bosanac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, last time I explained to you why the Trial Chamber had decided to have her as a 92 ter witness, because she was going to speak to the evacuation of the hospital, her arrest, very little about Ovcara, and she was not going to testify about volunteers, let alone about volunteers from the SRS. So the Trial Chamber thought that it was not necessary to devote too much time to her testimony, because what mattered was to know whether there was shelling or not of the hospital, what she saw, what was said about the evacuation, and, thirdly, what happened following the evacuation. It so happens that, and there you're right in saying so, that the Prosecutor took some time to have a few documents admitted into evidence. These were lists brought by the witness and then connected with a number of victims, so the witness had to be shown the documents. There were questions by the Judges because there is a list that is attached to the indictment, so we had to make some checks. After this, the Judges and myself, we put questions to the witness. She said things that were not to be found in the written statement, and for the sake of justice, for justice to be done and to be manifested, we had to put questions in order to shed some light on some issues. That was necessary for the Prosecution case, but also for your case. This is why some verifications had to be carried out. And it's true that in the end, she said that she'd heard you speaking on the radio, something that she had not said in the written statement. Whether she did hear it or not, whether she mixed it up or not, we thought it was not necessary to dwell on the matter. So this being said, this is how things happened. Now you say that the Serbian public opinion knows who the witness is. I do not know anything at all about her. I do not know what people may think of what she did. But if you had cross-examined her, you could have put it to her. You could have said, "Madam, you said this," or that, "Here is a book written by an individual or by myself," I don't know, I think you also wrote a book about Vukovar, "and this is said in this book." You could have given her a page number, and then she could have answered to say whether she agreed or not, and that would have been a legal proceeding, rather than you waiting until the end, precisely at the moment when I thanked her for coming to testify, for having this outburst, for putting down her testimony in a matter of three lines. So this is how things happened. The Trial Chamber wishes to remind you that Rule 92 ter allows you to cross-examine. It allows us to save time. There's no need to spend too much time on Prosecution questions whilst there is a statement. The witness can just say, "Yes, I confirm -- I can confirm what I said earlier on." The witness is then shown a few documents. Thereafter, you are free to cross-examine. It is geared towards judicial economy. Well, we have heard you, and this is your point of view, your stance on the 92 ter proceeding. Unfortunately, this is bound to happen again, because we are going to hear some 92 ter witnesses; for instance, the very next witness to testify. The Judges read the statement. I read the next witness's statement. They identify the questions -- the relevant questions that are to be asked that are relevant in view of the indictment, and through our questions we're going to ascertain -- check some of the things that are mentioned. We do not take for granted what is written in the written statement. It's not gospel to us. So you could say, "Okay, that's not how I see things. I don't just accept the written statement. There is a written statement that I want to check as to its contents, its sum," especially when it has to do with alleged crimes, with the alleged involvement of volunteers in such crimes, with the role of the JNA, of the TO, with the role of political leaders of the municipality, if applicable. That's the type of question that we put to a witnesses, that's the general format. There's nothing -- no mystery about it. And we also want to know whether there was any impact of speeches you made in a given municipality or location. Look at the questions we have put so far. We basically used this format to check what witnesses say, even if some questions are not dealt with. If we have a witness here, we may as well use that witness for truth to be really expressed. This is the purpose of our questions. When your turn comes, because you said that you were going to testify, what questions will be put to you, rest assured that you will have questions put by the Judges, because they want to re-thrash it out. And when you call your own witnesses, we will put similar questions, based on the same format, to your witnesses. Whether they are Defence or Prosecution witnesses, we have the same type of questions. Of course, there may be tangentially this or that might change, depending on their occupation, the position of a witness, whether that witness is a military or a civilian person, but basically it's the same type of questions because they do contribute to justice being done. Let's have VS-1131 brought in. I'm not quite sure, Mr. Ferrara. How much time have you planned for this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I just say one thing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. How much time?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: He's a 92 ter witness, too, as well, so half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Half an hour. Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just one brief objection concerning what you said; namely, that the role of the Rule 92 ter is to save time. I absolutely disagree with it, because it has become evident, after all these witnesses who are viva voce, that not a single one was capable of repeating what is in their alleged statement, not even those who make their best effort to be cooperative with the Prosecution. The statements reflect what the Prosecution wanted the statement to contain, not what the witness had to state. But the essential question here is: Why didn't the Prosecutor think to put all the questions you asked into the statement of this witness? He could have done ten times more. He could have put in everything that the Croatian propaganda for the past 20 years, if you ask me, had put out in the public. They could have put it all in the statement of Vesna Bosanac. They could have led it all. Her intelligence is not to be underestimated, but her lack of moral fibre, either, shouldn't be underestimated. I told you several times that in my view, she's one of the key Prosecution witnesses, and I kept insisting all the time how important it was for her to testify viva voce. Now, you asked me why I don't cross-examine 92 ter witnesses. I don't cross-examine them because that would be a subsequent legalisation of their 92 ter testimony, and I'm convinced that if I refuse to cross-examine them, that will be later a key proof of the irregularity of this trial, because nowhere in the world can a witness's testimony go directly into evidence if the Defence is unable to cross-examine when the statement was taken at first and in the courtroom. This rule was introduced only in 2006, and the indictment against me was brought in 2003, so there is no legal foundation and I am prejudiced by this. That's why I refuse to cross-examine them. I don't want to lose this important, vital argument in contesting the whole process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, this discussion took place quite a while ago. We are aware of your position. Let's have the witness brought in. It's already 20 to 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, while that's being done, clearly, just so there's no surprise for the accused in the future, the position that we take and will continue to take is that each and every time, he is waiving his right to cross-examine, and that's the end of the story. Clearly, cross-examination can be waived, and that's exactly what's happened. So there is no violation of his rights, as a result of his own informed decision to waive that cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please state your first name, surname, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Milorad Vojnovic. I was born on the 15th of October, 1945, in Gorica village, Sipovo municipality, currently in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. Do you have a current occupation or are you retired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Retired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what was your occupation before, in which corps were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I retired as a JNA officer, that is, an officer of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was your rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Colonel, have you had an opportunity to testify before a court of law as to the events in the former Yugoslavia or is this the first time you're going to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have testified before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In which case, where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I testified in Belgrade and in The Hague. The case was Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it was in the Ovcara case in Belgrade and in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In The Hague, it was the trial of the three; Sljivancanin, Mrksic and Radic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I suppose that each and every time, you were a Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last question before I ask you to read the solemn declaration. We're going to see your written statement made on the 11th of September, 2008. But prior to the statement, did anyone exert pressure on you for you to testify in one way or another, or were you never the object of pressure, did anyone call you to say that you had to say certain things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
