utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was regularly asked to testify in Belgrade, and I have received invitations from The Hague as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you were called by the Office of the Prosecutor, never called by anyone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And before, I had calls from the Defence, but later from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said before, it was calls from the Defence. From which Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Previously, I cooperated in the -- with the Defence in the Vukovar Three case, and now I am where I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So initially you were a Defence witness for one of the three accused in the Vukovar case, and then later on you became a Prosecution witness, is that so, unless in the Vukovar trial you testified as a Defence witness. I don't know. Were you a Defence witness? Who were you a witness for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were you a Prosecution witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But before you were a Prosecution witness, you worked with the Defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's now clear. Please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. You may be seated. Witness, you are testifying under Rule 92 ter. I'm sure that the Prosecutor explained things to you, he's going to put a number of questions to you and submit also a number of documents. He's scheduled to take about 30 minutes to do so. Afterwards, the Judges sitting in front of you will probably put questions to you. I, myself, I have questions for you, and my colleagues may have questions for you as well. Mr. Seselj should not put any questions to you, because he has decided, as a matter of course, not to cross-examine witnesses testifying under Rule 92 ter. This is what I wanted to explain to you in order for this hearing to proceed as smoothly as possible. Mr. Ferrara, you have the floor. You're going to give us a brief summary of the witness's testimony and also to put the usual questions, questions relevant to this 92 ter proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I start with the court summary. Milorad Vojnovic is a retired JNA colonel, as he said. From September 1991 to March 1995, he was in command of the Kragujevac-based 80th Motorised Brigade. On 29 October 1991, the Motorised Brigade began deploying in Eastern Slavonia under the command of Operational Group South. Witness brigade deployment was completed around the 7th of November, 1991. Neither of his units participated directly in combat operations. Their task was to cover the area during the period while other more experienced units carried out specific combat missions. After the takeover of the town of Vukovar towards the end of November 1991, the 1st Motorised Brigade left the town, and the witness was appointed town commander by Colonel Mrksic. In January 1992, the 80th Motorised Brigade left Eastern Slavonia, but the witness brigade remained in the area until 28 February 1992. "Colonel Vojnovic personally witnessed the arrival of volunteers in the area, and he learned some of these volunteers that tried to join regular forces were often removed after only a few days because they were mainly interested in looting. "The witness attended daily briefings of the Operational Group South command. He saw Arkan in one of these meetings in October or November 1991 before the fall of the town, meeting that was held in the command post of the 1st Military District and attended by all the important commanders. He saw again Arkan in official meetings with General Zivota Panic and General Andrija Biorcevic in January 1992 to discuss the situation in the Vukovar area. "After the fall of Vukovar, volunteers and TO members were integrated into one detachment and put under the command of the 80th Brigade. "Concerning the events occurred in Ovcara, the witness was not aware that the hospital in Vukovar would be evacuated. On the evening of 20th November 1991, he was on his way to a meeting when he passed by the hangar in Ovcara. There, he saw at least two buses from the hospital and the gauntlet formed by members of the local TO, people in civilian clothes and people wearing different uniform garments as well as Chetniks insignia, a gauntlet which the evacuees had to pass through in order to enter the hangar. Before entering the hangar, the prisoners were confiscated of their belongings, hit, beaten, even using weapons, and cursed. The witness tried to address the people in the gauntlet, trying to make them stop. Later on, he went on to try -- trying to physically protect the prisoners, and for this reason he was insulted and addressed, 'What are you doing, old man, what do you want? These are our prisoners,' he was told. "Inside the hangar, the witness saw several officers from the 1st Motorised Brigade, which led him to believe they were in charge of the evacuation. He was shocked by the atmosphere and by the maltreatment he personally witnessed inside the hangar. He continued his efforts to stop them, but after 30 minutes he had to leave for a briefing with Colonel Mrksic. During his meeting with Mrksic, the witness raised the issue of a maltreatment of prisoners at the Ovcara hangar, and Mrksic replied, 'Don't talk about this.' This made the witness believe that Mrksic was aware of what was going on. "After the meeting, he tried to approach again Mrksic, and the answer that there was a complex situation and that military police was pushed back at the hangar. When the witness returned from his command post, he learned that the military police withdrew from the hangar and a decision had been made to hand the prisoners over to the TO. "The witness does not remember whether Milan Lancuzanin, also known as Kameni, was at the hangar, but he later learned that he was there. However, after the fall of the town, he cooperated with Kameni and his unit to form a group to search for broken weapons. The witness was aware that Kameni had been awarded the title of vojvoda by Vojislav Seselj and was in charge of one paramilitary unit. The witness met Seselj himself at a celebration of the first anniversary of the liberation of Vukovar on 18 November 1992. The witness heard that Seselj had visited Vukovar in November 1991, but he did not meet him on that occasion." Your Honours, this concludes my summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a problem. It may be related to translation. Listening to the translation in French, I heard that Kameni was in charge of a Territorial Defence unit, whereas if I look at the transcript in English, I read "a paramilitary unit." What did you say, Mr. Ferrara?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: "Paramilitary unit," Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Colonel, did you meet with any member of the Office of the Prosecutor on the 11th September 2008?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I do not remember having met with a representative of the OTP, but in 2008 I met with the chief of the Security Administration. As for a representative of the OTP, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did you meet with me and an investigator on 11th September 2008?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: You?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I made a mistake. Yes, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did you sign a statement on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did you review the statement before signing it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: In which language?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: In the Serbo-Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Could we please have the document with 65 ter number 7325 on the screen, and give the hard copy to the witness, please, Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Colonel, could you please look at the first page of the statement, the B/C/S version. Do you recognise your signature at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Could you now flip through the pages of the statement and tell me whether you recognise your initials there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise my initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Could you now look at page 16 of the statement. It should be the last one -- the one before the last.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: The 17th page of the witness Statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Yes. Do you recognise your signature at the bottom of that page?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Does this statement accurately reflect the events that you describe in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: If you were asked questions about those events today, would you give the same answer as contained in the statement, that are contained in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I would probably give the same answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Thank you. You don't need to look at the copy of this document. Your Honours, I would like to seek for the admission into evidence of this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to give it a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P604, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honour, you're aware that attached to this statement is a table containing several documents, and I will put questions to the witness concerning these documents. Mr. Registrar, can we have on the screen the document 65 ter number 728. Can you show him the first page? I mean, we could give him a copy, too. There are a lot of pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Colonel, can you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: This is a standard war diary form which is maintained by commands of a certain level.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to see this document before?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: The first -- this is the first time that I see this document, now with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Today or when you signed the statement?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly whether it was today or when I signed the statement, but, yes, I have seen this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can you tell us if there is any reference in this document to the involvement of volunteers units in the combat area? For example, I would like that you -- that you check this page, and if the usher can put it on the screen. It is the ERN page in the B/C/S version 0293-5446.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what page that is in this document before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: You can check the document, and I think at the top of the page should be -- you should find this number, or maybe we can put it on the ELMO if the usher -- it maybe is easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ferrara, can you please give us the page number in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. I'm sorry I didn't make it before. It's page L000107. It is the third entry dated 4 October at hour 1430.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Colonel, can you -- can you read for us this third entry on the page?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The 4th of October, 1430, some 40-odd volunteers have come from Belgrade, and they were sent to the 2nd Motorised Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ferrara, we have a problem here, because in English we have L0100501, 502 and so on and so forth. We don't have that 107 page. Secondly, if I go to the page corresponding to the 4th of October, I can't find the entry for 1430 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: I repeat the number. Maybe there is some problem, because I have the ERN in English. It's page L0100507.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have this page in English. Okay, yes, we can see the entry for the 4th of October. But, Mr. Ferrara, the problem is that the 4th of October comes after -- it comes after the 6th of October, and militarily speaking, this is impossible. Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: You should ask who drafted it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the colonel may be able to tell us why.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I cannot confirm the authenticity of this document, because at that time I had not yet arrived in that area, but I can only read what it says here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, you served in the JNA as an officer, and we know that the JNA abided by strict rules. Is it understandable and normal that in such a war diary, we should have the entries related to the 4th of October after the entries related to the 6th of October?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not what I'm saying. I'm saying that this is not the war diary of my unit. That's why I say I can't confirm its authenticity. Otherwise, it says very clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, we find an entry related to Negoslavci village, the 6th of October. We have something for 1600 hours. Then for 1610. At 4.30, we have Air Force jets which fired. We have something else that happened at 5.30 p.m., and then we move on to the 4th of October at 11.00 a.m. So why is it that we move to the 4th of October after the 6th of October?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say that with any certainty. I'm saying this is not our war diary, it was not kept by my unit, so I cannot make any particular comment. I can't make out what it says, and I don't know what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Could such a thing have happened in your unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it wouldn't have happened. It was kept regularly with indication of time, date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can you read this one?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Ferrara. Apparently this document -- this document is not a document that the witness can tell us very much about, because it's not a document that was produced by his unit. You can only put questions to the witness about the contents of this document if he's aware of this. If not, then it's a bit tricky.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have a colonel of the JNA, as you said, that can say how the war diary is drafted or not. This is the reason we want to tender this document through this witness, because of course we cannot call Major -- Colonel Mrksic to testify concerning this war diary. So we have a colonel of the JNA, and I think he can say as --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The witness may only testify about what he had seen himself or heard himself, that is, his direct knowledge. He's not here as an expert to be asked to interpret whether the document is authentic or not and whether its contents reflect historical facts. What Mr. Ferrara is doing is really scandalous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ferrara, you are telling us that Colonel Mrksic cannot testify. Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... cannot testify. I told that here we have a colonel of the JNA, so maybe we can try to tender this document through him, an interpretation of this document by this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. We are going to consider the matter. No, the Trial Chamber does not agree with you. We do not accept this. Please move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: We'll continue with other documents, Your Honour. Mr. Registrar, can you display on the screen the document bearing 65 ter number 854, and we can go to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Here on the document, it says: "Report on an extraordinary incident submitted to the 1st Military District." It says that: "Around midnight, in a settlement called Holivud in Vukovar, three members of the Territorial Defence of Vukovar were killed." Shall I go on reading? Is this enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: It's enough. Are you familiar with the incident in question?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I did not know about the incident then. I learned about it later. The first time I learned about it was when I testified in Belgrade. It is, indeed, a desk officer from my brigade, but I'm not sure if this was really done.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: We read in this document that the killed men were the members of Leva Supoderica Detachment under the command of Milan Lancuzanin, known as Kameni, and the document is dated 22nd December 1991. Does it mean that the Leva Supoderica unit or detachment was still existing in December 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: The document dates back to that year, indeed. These problems did exist. I did not learn about this incident then. If I had known about it, I would have probably reacted in some way. I really don't know whether this incident happened. This was written by my desk officer for security, bypassing our command, without our knowledge, and he sent it to the 1st Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: But you did not answer my question. Did it mean that Leva Supoderica unit still existed in December 1991 in Vukovar and that Milan Lancuzanin, also known as Kameni, was in charge of the Leva Supoderica unit, as we read in this document?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the Leva Supoderica unit did -- no longer existed at that time. Perhaps there were people, ex-members of that unit, who stayed there and maybe called themselves that, but the unit did not exist. I know that for sure, because Milan Lancuzanin came to my Command, and I remember him. He cooperated with us very well. I said already it was a family that was wealthy and well thought of in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, this is important, very important indeed. We have a document that, by all signs, is a document, a military document. It has a stamp, names, and numbers. Whilst I'm listening to you, what you say prompts a whole host of questions in my mind. In 1991, in December 1991, if I understand properly, you were appointed a commander in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you were then the Vukovar commander. In other words, you had authority over all of the military units in Vukovar. We agree on this, don't we?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It so happens that on the 22nd of December, there were two soldiers who were TO members in Vukovar that were killed. We do not know by whom they were killed. Now, you, as the commander in Vukovar, did you have authority over the Vukovar TO in December, that is, militarily speaking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Since you were the number 1, as it were, for military forces in Vukovar, if two soldiers were killed, would such an event be automatically made known to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the incident was of the nature that I should have been informed, but I wasn't. You see that the document was written by the security officer, who sent it to the superior command, not us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this security officer, that was Lieutenant Colonel Vasic, do you know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he was Second Lieutenant Vasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So did you know this second lieutenant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know him that well because he was from the reserve. He never informed me of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that since you were the military person in charge, you would meet with your officers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I met with officers regularly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You had regular meetings. If two soldiers from a unit are killed by unknown authors, I suppose that is going to be mentioned by a lieutenant, a captain or a commander, unless there were so many killed at the time that that would not even be mentioned in a meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it was not mentioned at any meetings. I'm sure about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your view, is this an authentic document or do you have doubts as to the authenticity of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot claim anything now with any degree of certainty, but we see his signature here and we see the stamp of my unit, and this should be all right. But I'm telling you, I can't be certain, because I saw this document for the first time many years later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Back then in December 1991, did Milan Lancuzanin, also known as Kameni, was this man under your authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That December, perhaps a few days after this, we set up a detachment which included all the members of the Territorial Defence. I can't remember for sure whether Kameni was among them, but I know he came regularly to the Command, and after these events I had no problems whatsoever with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This Leva Supoderica unit, did it exist in December 1991? Take your time before your answer, because this is an extremely relevant question. So take all the time you need. I'll repeat the question. Did the Leva Supoderica unit exist in December 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the unit Leva Supoderica did not exist then as a unit, an officially organised, registered unit. That did not exist. Maybe there were individuals who believed themselves to be members of that unit, but the unit did not exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question. In the event that this is an authentic document and that you did not see it because that eluded you or because your subordinate officers did not mention it to you, how is it possible that a second lieutenant, who's a security officer, so he has some competence or jurisdiction, how can he write that the two people, the two soldiers that were killed, were members of that detachment, of the Leva Supoderica Detachment, that was under the command of Milan Lancuzanin, aka Kameni, and that therefore the military police and the SUP were investigating the case? How can this man write this whilst apparently the unit no longer existed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the unit didn't exist for sure. This is an action taken by the second lieutenant and perhaps another security officer who is superior to him, without our knowledge, and the report they sent circumvented us. That's how this security service operated, bypassing the Command, and I don't think that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I won't interfere with your examination, but I have to draw your attention to the fact that I discovered a very important falsification in this so-called document, because we have no proof of its authenticity. In paragraph 3 of the original, it says the persons killed are from the Leva Supoderica unit under the command of Captain Milan Lancuzanin, aka Kameni, whereas in the English translation we read: [In English] "Members of Leva Supoderica Detachment under the command of Milan Lancuzanin, aka Kameni." [Interpretation] It's very symptomatic that the English translation omits the rank of Kameni, captain. He is a reserve captain of the JNA still on active duty at the time. Why was that omitted from the English translation? And we know that the Registry is responsible here for veracity of translation. It's very important that we know that he's an officer, and that as an officer, he was appointed a commander of a unit. He was a JNA officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, the accused has just noted that in the B/C/S document, Kameni's rank is mentioned. He's a captain. It's not to be found in the English translation. As far as you can remember, was Kameni a captain or not? Because if he was a captain, the security officer, who's a lieutenant, he knows what the captain is, as a rank. What do you have to say to that? Was he a captain or not? Because it is written in B/C/S that he was a captain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand the question. I see that it's written, but I really didn't know if he had the rank of captain. He came to see me without any insignia indicating that he was an officer. I did not know he was an officer -- he was a captain at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, if he was a captain, when you would meet with your officers, a captain would be present, by right, unless he was ill?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. Nobody came to our meetings we had within the framework of the brigade, nobody from the Territorial Defence or anyone else. He came to see me on his own when he had time, to get advice or assistance, but I never saw him displaying the rank of captain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But, Colonel, when TO units are subordinated to the JNA, whenever there's a briefing, the commander of the TO unit, the officer would attend the meeting, because you had authority and control, or you're supposed to have control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They did not come to our meetings. They formed some other units. They were assigned to some other duties mainly around the town, helping around. They did not exist as organised units until a new detachment was formed in December. And once they were formed, they were disbanded, they went home, and they were ready to take up duty if called up. At that time, the police had been established and the executive branch of the authorities in Vukovar existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your view, why did Lieutenant Vasic say that he was a captain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say now. I don't know whether he, himself, knew him to be a captain, but I see that it's written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. You have already used 27 minutes, Mr. Ferrara, so you have very little time left.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another objection to make. I believe it is the duty of the Prosecutor to explain why the indication of rank is left out of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Of course I can't explain, because I'm not a translator, but I believe the accused should be informed this kind of issue can be raised in the correct phase of the trial, that is, the cross-examination. When you object during an examination-in-chief, you object a question of the Prosecutor. I didn't put any question, so he objects, so he's using the time of the Prosecution to cross-examine the witness concerning these documents. Maybe he should do this in the correct phase, that is, the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right in saying so, Mr. Ferrara, but the problem is that we may, maybe, have some doubt as to this document. We have a translation into English, as Judges. I don't know where it comes from. I can see "OTP/MAT." Is this translation made by somebody from the OTP or is this a CLSS translation? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: I was told by our case manager that "OTP/MAT," what does it mean, "Military Analyst Team."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The translation was done by the Military Analyst Team. You can understand that this is not void of interest. We have two possibilities. Either this document is authentic, in which case Lancuzanin, aka Kameni, is a captain, a JNA captain. If he's a captain, he is under the authority of the JNA, or he's not a captain - this is what the witness seems to indicate - in which case it's a very fuzzy situation, from the legal point of view, and we can have some doubt as to the document then. As you can see, I personally believe that very relevant documents have to be translated by our service, by the Tribunal services, CLSS, and not by the person seeking to tender the document. We are going to have a question by Judge Harhoff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Colonel, I would like to follow up on one of the questions posed to you by the Presiding Judge in respect of your description of the control or the command that you had over the Leva Supoderica unit or detachment. My question is: Was this detachment under the control of the JNA during the time when it was active in Vukovar in November 1991? And if it was, then was it under your control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Leva Supoderica Detachment was under the control of OG South, and later they were dismantled and were not under my control. They did not exist as a detachment after departure in December, their departure in December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. But when it was still active, that is to say in November 1991, was it then under your control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You tell us that it was under the control and command of the OG South. Who was in charge of the OG?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 1st Military District was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And who was in charge of the 1st Military District?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under the control of the OG South, the OG South had a commander, and the OG South was under the command of the military district. Colonel Mrksic was the commander of the OG South, and he was subordinated to the Command of the 1st Military District.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Was your brigade, the 80th Motorised Brigade, was that also a part of the OG South?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was, until the 1st Guards Brigade left for Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was from the 7th of November, when the brigade came, up to the time the brigade left for Belgrade, until the 25th of November or thereabouts, the 25th or the 26th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And during that time, I assume that you, as the commander of your brigade, would take part in meetings that were convened by Colonel Mrksic in the OG, and these meetings would presumably also include the commander of the Leva Supoderica Detachment, would it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I attended those meetings, but I did not see them there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But it seems to me that it is strange that a detachment that was under the command of the OG did not take part in the meetings. How is that to be understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they were not directly subordinated to this OG. They were members of some other subordinated units, so battalions in other units from the Operation Group South. That is why they were not present at the regular briefings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So to which units was the Leva Supoderica Detachment then subordinated within the OG South?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say with precision to what unit it was subordinated. Perhaps to the 2nd Motorised Battalion, the 1st Motorised Battalion, or some other units in OG South. They had their own superiors before OG South. That is why they did not appear at briefings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one follow-up question, and then I'll give you the floor, Mr. Seselj. You said that the Leva Supoderica unit was dismantled. As far as you know, when? On what exact day was it dismantled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember exactly the date. I only know that it was dismantled, it was disbanded, after the departure of a part of the OG South, i.e., the 1st Guards Brigade to Belgrade. All these units ceased to exist as a part of the establishment, and they ceased to exist as units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, Mr. Seselj said on several occasions that the said unit, the Leva Supoderica unit, had left Vukovar as soon as Vukovar had been taken; around the 17th or the 18th of November, he said. He added that people -- the men left in buses to return to Serbia, as I understood it. Some days ago, he said that he had eight statements made by bus drivers, so he thought that the few members of the Leva Supoderica unit that had stayed had stayed for their own reasons, because they were Vukovar residents, and since they were volunteers they had decided to stay. But is this consistent with what you knew of the situation at the time? It is a very complicated question, because that goes back in time several years ago, but these are pieces of information that I have and I'd like to seek your view on them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can claim with certainty that the Leva Supoderica Detachment at that time was not under my command, its activities totally unknown to me, and who left and whether anyone left, but a group did stay on of those men, among whom was Kameni, and what their role was, I cannot say. I cannot say anything specific. They were not under my command, so that's it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to go back to the previous problem, because my objection was purely of a procedural nature, and Mr. Ferrara is not right when he says that I should have presented it in cross-examination. Such an objection has nothing whatsoever to do with cross-examination, because it does not refer to the witness. Mr. Ferrara himself told us that these documents have been translated by the office of military experts, by their staff, so the conclusion I draw is that (redacted) of the OTP, deliberately falsified this document to omit the rank of Kameni so that the English translation would not show that he is an officer, a captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Here we have another problem, that the accused can continue to do -- behave in this way. He says that one of the witnesses of the Prosecutor forged the document, deliberately falsified this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Is it forged or is it not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Without saying that a specific individual forged the document, the Trial Chamber notes that the word "captain" is to be found in the B/C/S version, but it is not to be found in the English version. So anybody can draw the conclusions they like. You have a few minutes left before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: I ask to redact the sentence in the line 7, 8 and 9 concerning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to deliberate on this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I previously [as interpreted] present my position before you consult?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After discussing the matter, the Trial Chamber has decided not to redact those lines. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: (redacted). We do not know whether he did it or not, so no need to leave any doubt in this respect. But what Mr. Seselj said about the rest has to be left in the transcript. So, Madam Registrar, prepare a redacting order. You have a few minutes left, Mr. Ferrara, to finish the procedure of seeking to tender the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Yes. I want to point out that of course this is a draft translation of the document. We can ask for an official translation to the CLSS. And I'd like to move to move to seek the document into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to give an MFI number to this document, an MFI number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become Exhibit P605, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can we have on the screen the 65 ter number 723.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we'll have to redact what you've just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Exactly, I agree with you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see that when you are a Presiding Judge, you can't afford to take a nap. You have to be on your toes at every single moment. Madam Registrar, please prepare another redaction of the transcript. Mr. Ferrara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Colonel, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I do, but it's not exactly clear. Perhaps if it could be zoomed in on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can you zoom the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Could you tell us what -- who issued this order?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I think that I issued this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you intended to achieve with this order?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the departure of the 1st Guards Brigade, what I intended to do with this order was for the units in the entire area of the brigade to be secured, the Command to be secured, the units to be billeted in more comfortable quarters, since up to that time they were in some stables and sheds and other substandard accommodation, so that I wanted to transfer this number of units to better accommodation. And that also applied to other units whom I had relocated in order to enable -- to have them have better living conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Was this order addressed also to the TO unit?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot see the bottom of the page. I cannot see that. It was addressed to them, but as the TO staff of Vukovar is referred to here, I expect that it was also addressed to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: And to the volunteers?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, just to the Territorial Defence Staff of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to move the document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to give a number to this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P605, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't put any question concerning the document with the 65 ter number 709 attached to the statement because it's already admitted into evidence as Exhibit P41, for the record. And I ask the last question concerning the last document, the 65 ter number 701, if we have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to correct. The last exhibit is admitted under number P606.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Miss Registrar, can we have on the screen the 65 ter number 701.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Colonel, can you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document of OG South of the 20th of November, and it deals with the regulation of the issue of resubordination. It is an order which states that in order to unify the Command, we should resubordinate the armoured battalion of the 544th Motorised Brigade to the 80th Motorised Brigade. All issues with regard to the resubordination will be regulated by the Command of the 80th Motorised Brigade until they receive a new task. The armoured battalion of the 544th Motorised Brigade will be carrying out its task in compliance with the decision of 16 November 1991. And that was to relocate from the area of Jakobovac to another place, to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did this resubordination occur for the TO members and volunteers as well?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: It is not so stated in this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Do you know if it took place, even if it's not in this order, with another order?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot really claim that they were encompassed with this order, because it is spelled out precisely in this order that the armoured battalion would be transferred to my unit, and that is what was -- what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P607, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: I don't have further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to break for 20 minutes. After the break, I will have a number of questions to put to the witness. We'll resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The court is back in session. Colonel, I have a number of questions to put to you. First of all, I'm going to deal with the volunteers, and then, in a second stage, I'm going to deal with what you, yourself, saw at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First, the volunteers, the volunteers you saw arrive in the area at the time, were you aware of the fact that the volunteers, that's something that was provided for by the law at the time in the former Yugoslavia, because if someone had not been mobilised into the JNA, that person could declare himself as a volunteer? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the volunteers could gather, and once they gathered, they could join the JNA in an organised way and act under the JNA Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've had a lot of witnesses testify before us, including volunteers. Some of them told us that they were volunteers because they refused to serve in the ranks of the JNA, because for them the JNA was tantamount to the former communist system, and for them to join the JNA would be tantamount to supporting the communist system, whereas they, themselves, were royalists, liberals, and so on and so forth. Some of them told us that they wanted to fight for their country, but they did not want to do so under the JNA. They wanted to fight for their country as volunteers. What do you have to say about people who give such explanations?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think there were people of both kinds. Most of them joined the JNA and placed themselves under JNA command, and to a lesser extent there were others who did not want to subordinate themselves and acted independently, perhaps. I didn't know of any such cases in the territory of Vukovar, I don't know about any such groups, but I know they existed in other places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question follows up on your answer. Within the JNA, and considering the way it was organised, was it possible for the JNA to take part in military operations without controlling units that were fighting with the JNA, together with the JNA? In military terms, would such a thing be possible or completely impossible? And here I'm putting the question to a colonel of the JNA. I'm talking to a professional here.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the volunteers who were part of the JNA worked under JNA command, received assignments from their JNA officers, and did not act independently. They were involved, together with others, in combat operations and cooperated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We know that there were volunteer units, starting with Leva Supoderica, to mention only one. Talking now about the command of these units, would it be possible for such a volunteers unit to act independently in the field, independently of the chain of command? Would such a thing be technically possible and theoretically possible?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: According to the rules, that unit, which acted as part of the JNA, the Leva Supoderica unit, was subordinated to the JNA. I don't exclude the possibility of smaller independent groups existing, but they were not part of the JNA. Those groups were condemned by everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. You say that you do not exclude the possibility of smaller independent groups existing but that they were condemned by everyone. Let's assume that in your area of command, you find that you have individuals who do not obey your orders. What do you do as the commander of that particular area? What steps would you take to put an end to such a situation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: There were no such cases. In my unit, if there had been, they would have been removed from the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. At least your answers are extremely precise. Talking about Vukovar now, before you took command of the town in December, who was in charge in Vukovar? Who was the number 1 in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: The most responsible person in Vukovar at the time I arrived was the commander of Operative Group South.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And who was the commander of Operative Group South?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of Operative Group South at the time was Mile Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Would the commander of Operative Group South regularly organise meetings with his subordinate officers to prepare military operations and then to have debriefing operations following these operations? Would such a procedure be followed and applied?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: It was a military hierarchy, wherein meetings with Mile Mrksic were attended by his subordinates, where they received assignments, and then they conveyed these assignments to their own subordinates and agreed about operations. And among those, there were probably some volunteer units that were part of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about you; did you attend meetings presided by Colonel Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time of the takeover of Vukovar by the JNA, in your recollection, were there preparatory meetings before the Croats surrendered? Were there meetings organised in order to put an end to the siege of Vukovar and did you attend to such meetings? And I'm talking about putting an end to the siege, thanks to various military operations, and of deciding what was to be done with prisoners. Did such meetings take place?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: These meetings were held regularly. My unit did not take part directly in the execution of operations. The commander issued assignments, specific assignments, to his units, such as capturing a street, one part of the town, and similar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are telling me that yourself and your unit did not take part directly in the fall of Vukovar, because you had not been given a task to deal with what was going to happen after the fall of Vukovar. It's something you had nothing to do with?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we did not know about the operation that would be carried out, not specifically in each unit, but I was present when the commander issued assignments to specific units regarding certain locations, certain streets, certain areas, how they were to be captured. They looked for ways how to carry out these operations, the combat, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was going to move on to something else, but you've just said something I find rather relevant. Let me put up a follow-up question to you. You stated that you took part in meetings where they decided how, the enemy, how the Croats were to be captured. In your recollection, during the such meetings would Colonel Mrksic tell his officers that they had to comply with the Geneva Conventions related to prisoners and with the law of the war and the way it was applied in the JNA? Would Colonel Mrksic remind his officers how important it was to comply with Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I was not present during discussions about capturing Croats, that is, members of the Croatian armed forces, but it is a fact that Colonel Mrksic pointed out the provisions of the Geneva Conventions and the appropriate treatment. In fact, every officer had a little manual on Geneva Conventions on him and how to treat prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me now move on to the second topic of my questions, i.e., Ovcara. I understand, when listening to you, that you just passed by, by chance. Can you explain to us what you were doing in the area?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I was going to Sotin, where I had one unit and one command to visit, and on my way back I also wanted to visit the command recently deployed at Ovcara. And that's when I saw, for the first time, that buses were coming and stopping outside the hangar. I didn't know what that was and who those people were, so I didn't actually stop to see the commander of the unit I was going to visit. I went straight to the hangar to see what was going on. I saw a couple of buses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me stop you here, because you've just said something that could be very relevant. I immediately noticed it, because nothing escapes me. You stated that you went to Sotin, and then you returned to Ovcara because the command had been deployed at Ovcara. Does that mean that the superior authority had decided that there should be a command post at Ovcara, and you were aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No. My unit was deployed in Sotin. That was one command, and another was in Ovcara. It was not originally planned that way, but because of some problems that occurred, I placed it at Ovcara, and it stayed there with the consent of the organ of the superior command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've just given us a very relevant piece of information. You, yourself, decided to place a command post at Ovcara. My fellow Judge would like to know, and I'm interested as well to know, when exactly, on what day you set up a command post at Ovcara, on what date exactly?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't set it up separately, but under a general order a command post was placed in various villages and locations, and their job was to help those people in the villages to organise themselves, to protect themselves and defend themselves, to get the water supply working, et cetera. That's why this commanding officer in Ovcara was placed there, with that purpose. It was, in fact, a circular security system that the military apply in all environments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who was the commanding officer at Ovcara that you had placed there? Who was it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I think that commanding officer who was in charge doesn't want his name mentioned. He was here as a protected witness, but we know who he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You don't want to tell us his name. Did he have soldiers with him, this officer? How many people were there with him?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he had perhaps six or seven soldiers servicing the command, couriers, messengers, signalsmen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you saw buses, people, and you saw how these people were being mistreated, so you intervened, you went inside the building. Can you tell us what you saw inside the building?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, inside the building, which is a hangar, there were people, and I didn't know where these people hailed from because that particular mission bypassed me. I had nothing to do with that order from the Command. Those people were to the left of the hangar, cordoned off. On the other side of the cordon, there were members of the Territorial Defence. I approached one commanding officer who was from the superior command and asked him, "Who are these people? Where are they from?" And that's when he told me that they were captives from the hospital. As I entered -- as they entered the hangar, they were mistreated. They had to run the gauntlet. They were beaten, kicked, insulted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there's a question that straight away crosses my mind. So there is this officer with six or seven soldiers with him and this is a command post that you have established. Had the JNA controlled the entire operation, that is, the prisoners as they were being evacuated from the hospital, who were supposed to be at Ovcara for a certain period of time, that brings about logistical and security problems, so within the military order should you have been informed because, after all, you yourself -- well, "you," your unit had a command post there. As part of a classical military operation, should you have been informed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I did not take part in this operation, either in the preparatory stage, or the organising, or the execution, neither I nor my Command nor my soldiers were involved. Such operations were executed without the knowledge of anyone, and I suppose for the news not to spread, we were not informed. But as I came close to the site, I found out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when you discovered that, what did you think straight away? What did you think of, you? You were a military man, you were in charge of things there. What did you think?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I was surprised to be ignorant of this situation and this event, because, after all, I was a brigade commander. My commands were in the immediate vicinity. I took measures to secure these people, and I informed my superior of all that I saw. I took measures to protect these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we speak about you informing Colonel Mrksic: You saw what was happening inside. We're not going to go into details. We are aware of them, and you spoke about them. So you came out of the hangar. Did you then see military police members?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know how it was? There were soldiers who had military belts, but whether they were members of the military police or not, I didn't know, because not all of them were from my units. But a part of my own military police came later to help organise, to help restore order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's speak about the people who were there. It seems that there were JNA members, TO members, civilians - one can wonder what they were doing there - and there were also volunteers. Can you confirm that the people I've just listed were present? I'll say it again very slowly: JNA members, Vukovar Territorial Defence members, volunteers, and civilians. Did you see people from these four categories?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I think I can confirm all of this. The only thing I didn't know then was that volunteers were also there. They were all dressed in the uniform -- the combined uniform of the Territorial Defence, so at that moment I didn't know who belonged to whom. There were members of the JNA, there were civilians wearing all sorts of dress, pieces of one and pieces of another, so it was not very clear who was a member of what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about the civilians; where did they come from? Were they coming out of the basements, where they had sought refuge and shelter for some time? Were they coming from their neighbouring villages? What were they doing there, if you know at all?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: You're talking about civilians?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the civilians you saw. Where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I think that those were civilians from the area of the hospital and also probably from the nearby villages who came to watch and to participate in the action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were there on the spot, and we heard witnesses who, too, were there. We heard victims as well, so we know a lot already. You were there. Therefore, as far as you can remember, what was the atmosphere like? Was it complete chaos, anarchy, or did you have the feeling that it was all very well organised?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I think that it was all organised, from the bringing of the people from the hospital up to the hangar, and in the hangar inside, it was already problematic. The situation was very complex. There was beating, there was hitting, there was insults, abuse. I could see that some people knew each other. They called out to each other by name or by surname. So the situation within the hangar was complex.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whether it was organised to take prisoners from one point to the other, yes, you need a certain degree of organisation. But as I understand it, when I say "organised," what I mean is all this beating and ill-treatment, was it organised or was this just some sudden upsurge of collective violence by the people who were there, who were taking revenge on the prisoners? How do you analyse the situation? How did you analyse the situation back then, and how do you analyse it now?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that there was no organised beating of the people. There were no commands issued to the effect of hit or beat. These were individual actions on the part of individuals who were embittered, who were disillusioned, who had grudges, mutual grudges. There were no commands to that effect, as -- for that to be done. Now, as I recall it, of course, it was very wrong to treat the prisoners in that way, but that is the way it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this really what you feel deep down?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: It is my deep conviction that I can never, of course, support someone beating some other people without those other people being able to resist or to strike back, because these people passed through the gauntlet and they had no weapons or anything to defend themselves with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you were about to leave. Did you pass by your Command first? Did you go to see the officer who was there with six or seven soldiers from your unit? Did you go and see him?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, because the moment he saw me, he was waiting there for me to inform me about the situation in his unit. I did not stay for any length of time with him. I went right -- I went to this place to see what was happening, because I was surprised by what was taking place. So he came from his area and gave us assistance, and he protected me and himself and, as far as he was able, the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about the six or seven soldiers from your unit; where were they?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: They were there with their superiors, and they helped as much as they can in order to stop the excesses, the beatings. They looked on, what was happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You got back into your car?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I got back in my vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you have a Motorola or a telephone, any means of communication with the Command?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, not at that time, because I had not expected anything of the kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you had absolutely no means at all?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what did you do? What time was it when you left?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: When I left, it was already time for my regular briefing, and I briefed my superior about the situation in Ovcara, about what I had seen, and how surprised at it I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What time did you leave Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say with precision what time it was, because nobody consulted their watches then, but people were trying to do something about it to help those people. I know that it was dark when I arrived at Mrksic's place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So night had fallen already. You went straight away to the Command, where you met with Colonel Mrksic, and this is important, as you can imagine. I assume that the questions I'm asking you must have been asked of you during the Belgrade trial and also in the Mrksic trial, but I have neither transcript. This is why I'm asking the questions that might have been asked of you before. Please explain how you met Colonel Mrksic. And your answer is of the utmost relevance. What did you tell him and what is he going to tell you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I entered the Command, to Mrksic's office. I was a bit late because of the event that I had seen there, and on that account I had stayed there a bit longer. I informed him about the situation in Ovcara, what was being done there, how the prisoners were being beaten and all the rest, and he told me, "Do not talk to me about it." So I understood that he actually knew what the situation was, and what was happening there, and who the people there were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he said to you, "Don't talk to me about it." You are on a very familiar basis. Were you friends or acquaintances, or did he speak politely to you, like, "Do not speak to me about this"? Did you have some friendly ties or was it just professional ties you had with him?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Ours was a professional relationship. He was my commander, he was my superior, and only a top commanding officer could have been the commander of the Guards Brigade. And we had only known each other for a short time. He said to me on two times, "Do not talk to me about it."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he spoke on a friendly basis to you. You heard this from your superior, and you know that things are happening that are banned by the military code, so what did you think then?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: At that moment, I did not know exactly what was happening, but I realised that he knew about it. This entire arrangement had been an unknown to me, this bringing of the people to Ovcara, but I could see that he was aware of it, for had the situation been any different, he would certainly have asked me what it was, what was being done, but he didn't ask anything of the kind. The only thing he said to me was, "Don't talk to me about it."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When he told you, "Don't speak to me about it," does that mean that he took on him the entire responsibility or that he knew but he was totally overwhelmed because of the civilians, the Territorial Defence, the volunteers and all the rest? What was your feeling? Did you have a feeling that he controlled the situation because he was the number 1 of the OG South, or was he totally just overwhelmed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I think that he was aware of the situation, because he had his organs and his commands in the hangar, but he probably did not know that it would get out of control to such an extent at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In such a situation, I am not going to read out to you all the rules of the military code. I could do so, but I'll go straight to the chase, cut to the chase. In such a situation where a subordinate officer informs his superior that there is a grave, very serious situation, and that the superior obviously fails to do anything, what does a JNA officer have to do, in view of the then applicable military code? I'm not trying to embarrass you, please do understand that, but I'd like you to give us a technical -- a military answer.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I think that I behaved as a professional officer. I informed my superior of the situation as I had found it. It was for him to inform his superior about the situation that he had been informed about or had come to know in some other way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in the chain of command, if a subordinate officer sees that his superior is unable to carry out his duty or commits a crime, is the subordinate officer not obliged to refer it to the rung above, and who was above Colonel Mrksic in the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: His superior was General Zivota Panic, the commander of the 1st Military District, and my security organ, via the security line, informed our security group which was relocated there and monitored the entire situation in Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So General Panic was informed via the security line of what was happening. You, you did not deem it necessary to go in person to see General Panic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, that was not to be done, because I didn't know what was going to happen, what the situation was like, what was going to be done with those people, because no one could have anticipated that what actually happened would happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One can easily imagine what happened. So your officer who was present in Ovcara, with the seven soldiers who'd stayed there, did they tell you that -- later, that is, that the people who were in the hangar left it and were taken in groups of 20 on board a tractor? Did they tell you that little by little the hangar was emptied out? Did your subordinates tell you that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No one of my commanding officers or men was there at that time when the people were being taken out of the hangar, nor did they see that, because this Command which was near the hangar, it was not actually that near, it was some 800 metres away, and it was a dark night, so that nobody saw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us move for a few moments to private session, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you heard. You'll have to tell us when you heard that. You heard there had been executions in the hangar. When did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see that, and I heard this from the lawyers in some of these -- the lawyers on the Defence team in some of these pre-investigation stages of the procedure, because I cooperated with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. So you took over command in Vukovar in December. That is just a few days later, since the events took place ten days earlier. When you took over command, did nobody tell you, or was there no rumour, or did rumour reach you that there had been executions when you took over command? And do understand my questions. I'm not trying to embarrass you. That would be very easy for a Judge to do so. I'm not playing that game, so my questions are absolutely neutral. But I do have this question. You took your command ten days after the 20th of November. We know that on the 20th of November, you told Colonel Mrksic what had happened. When you took over command ten days later, did you not ask yourself what had become of the detainees?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I have to say that after that date, too, until the Guards Brigade returned to Belgrade, we came for regular briefings. Nothing was being said in the Command about that. However, I informed my own brigade command about these events. I did not hear it from my superior command, but from people, from civilians in Negoslavci. I heard from them about what had happened. I know that the superior commander later said that there would be a team of investigators and of experts that would be coming to investigate matters, examine the scene. And as he had already said that and secured all that, it was not for me to take any such action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, I'm going to tell you why I am amazed. You straight away reported to Colonel Mrksic after what you'd said. We know that you had an officer who was present on the spot, together with soldiers. Despite the fact that Colonel Mrksic did nothing about it and told you not to worry about it, did you not find any curiosity? Were you not curious enough to just make a phone call to your officer to know whether things had calmed down or what had happened? You didn't do it, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I did send an officer of mine to examine the situation. No, I was not calm, I was not at ease, and I wanted him to inform me what was -- what the situation there was like. And he told me that the situation was complex, that the soldiers had been moved away, and that they held no sway at all there, because there was a larger group of armed people there and those people wouldn't obey anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's 7.00 p.m. We need to adjourn. We'll proceed with your testimony tomorrow morning at 8.30. I still have a few questions to ask you. I believe that my fellow Judges have some questions for you as well, and the Prosecutor may have some questions as part of his redirect. Witness, you'll come back in this courtroom at 8.30. The rest of your testimony won't take very long, because we have another witness we want to hear tomorrow. Rest assured that your testimony will be completed tomorrow morning, but let me remind you that you took the solemn declaration and now you're a witness here to -- in the service of justice. You're not to have, as such, any contacts with the OTP, and I would like to advise you not to call anyone except members of your family. But even if you do so, do not say anything about your testimony. Just remain in your hotel room and try to avoid any contacts with anyone, except, of course, with your closest relatives. Mr. Ferrara, you wanted to say something? No, apparently. As you know, tomorrow morning we'll be sitting at 8.30 in this courtroom, and I would like to wish everyone a pleasant evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 6th day of November, 2008, at 8.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.01 p.m.,
